title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarial Training for Vision Transformers
claim: Generalization succeeds only when sample size times squared signal strength passes a threshold, with a sharp phase transition.
layout: 4 heatmap panels in a row; red threshold curve overlaid; shared colorbars
description: Four heatmaps sit side by side. The x-axis is signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the y-axis is sample size N. Each cell is colored by test accuracy on a viridis scale, with yellow for high and purple for low, and each panel has its own colorbar. Panels (a) and (b) show clean and robust accuracy on synthetic data. Panels (c) and (d) show clean and robust accuracy on real-world data. A red hyperbolic curve marks the N·SNR² threshold in each panel (500, 1000, 500 and 800). Accuracy is high (yellow) above and to the right of the curve and low (purple) below and to the left of it. Robust accuracy transitions are noisier and more purple than clean ones. The eye goes first to the yellow regions and the red curve. Captions below each panel read 'Clean Heatmap' or 'Robust Heatmap'.
caption: Clean and robust test accuracy under adversarial training across various signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and sample sizes (N). (a)&(b): results on synthetic data; (c)&(d): results on real-world data. High test accuracy is colored in yellow, whereas low test accuracy is colored in purple.
abstract: Despite the remarkable success of Vision Transformers (ViTs) across a wide range of vision tasks, recent studies have revealed that they remain vulnerable to adversarial examples, much like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). A common empirical defense strategy is adversarial training, yet the theoretical underpinnings of its robustness in ViTs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first theoretical analysis of adversarial training under simplified ViT architectures. We show that, when trained under a signal-to-noise ratio that satisfies a certain condition and within a moderate perturbation budget, adversarial training enables ViTs to achieve nearly zero robust training loss and robust generalization error under certain regimes. Remarkably, this leads to strong generalization even in the presence of overfitting, a phenomenon known as \emph{benign overfitting}, previously only observed in CNNs (with adversarial training). Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets further validate our theoretical findings.
